description_full: The Campbell's Company, together with its subsidiaries, engages in the manufacture and marketing of food and beverage products in the United States and internationally. It operates through Meals & Beverages, and Snacks segments. The Meals & Beverages segment engages in the retail and foodservice businesses in the United States and Canada. This segment provides Campbell's condensed and ready-to-serve soups; Swanson broth and stocks; pacific foods broth, soups and non-dairy beverages; Prego pasta sauces; Pace mexican sauces; Spaghettios pasta; Campbell's gravies, beans and dinner sauces; Swanson canned poultry; V8 Juices And Beverages; Campbell's Tomato Juice; Rao's Pasta sauces, dry pasta, frozen entrées, frozen pizza and soups; Michael Angelo's Frozen Entrées And Pasta Sauces; and Noosa Yogurts. The Snacks Segment Retails Pepperidge Farm Cookies, Crackers, Fresh Bakery and Frozen Products, including Goldfish Crackers, Snyder's of Hanover Pretzels, Lance sandwich crackers, Cape Cod potato chips, Kettle brand potato chips, late july snacks, Snack factory pretzel crisps, and other snacking products. This segment is also involved in the snacking, and meals and beverage retail business in Latin America. It sells its products through retail food chains, mass discounters, mass merchandisers, club stores, convenience stores, dollar stores, e-commerce and other retail, commercial and non-commercial establishments, and independent contractor distributors. The company was formerly known as Campbell Soup Company and changed its name to The Campbell's Company in November 2024. The Campbell's Company was founded in 1869 and is headquartered in Camden, New Jersey.

financial_summary: The Campbell's Company is a mid-cap consumer defensive business with a $6.8B market cap on $9.7B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 8% against a 6% cost of capital, which means the business barely earns its keep economically.

The business throws off $678M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 2.58× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, debt is heavy at 5.3× net debt/EBITDA, and leverage like that is what turns a bad year into a permanent loss, and thin 2.6× interest coverage leaves no room for a bad year.

Management returns a meaningful 7.3% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 40% of the shares, so management thinks like owners because it is one — the strongest alignment there is.

Slow-motion taste and channel shifts — private label, Gen-Z health preferences, or a DTC disruption can erode decade-old brand moats without a single dramatic quarter.
Input cost inflation from agricultural commodities — when raw materials spike, pass-through pricing lags and margin compression is immediate.
GLP-1 and health-trend demand destruction — weight-loss drugs and wellness shifts are structurally reducing consumption in snack, beverage, and packaged food categories.

sect: Its 9% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Defensive median (7%).
Its share of sector profits slightly exceeds its share of revenue (1.08x).
It accounts for 0.3% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been losing share of the sector profit pool (-13.6% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a steep downtrend, down 35% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 29% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 34% and a beta of 0.24, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.45 vs 5y 0.08), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $135.6M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 23% in the 2020 crash, 12% in the 2022 bear market and 35% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 39% below its DCF fair value of $37.24, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models corroborate one another (dispersion 3%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $22.26 to $61.74 (P10-P90).
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Defensive peers: P/FCF 10.0 vs 16.1 (sector median).
Against its own history it is cheap: the EBIT multiple sits 28% below its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are mixed: an FCF yield of 10.0% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 6.1% (vs the 8% bar).
The 17 covering analysts target $20.79 on average, 9% below the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 8% earns above the cost of capital of 6.0%, but the 2pp spread is short of the 7pp moat bar; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.47).
It converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 2.58x.
ROE of 10% is amplified by 4.1x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 1.0% of revenue on R&D and 0.6% on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is heavy at 5.3x net debt to EBITDA ($394.0M of cash against $7.1B of debt), and interest cover is thin at 2.6x.
Warning signs: an Altman Z of 1.52 in the distress zone.
The current ratio of 0.82 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 1.4% over 3 years, 2.8% over 5 years and 2.0% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 1% of profits supports about 0.1% a year of fundamental growth, too little to drive meaningful growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -2.3% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex roughly matches depreciation (0.9x, 3.7% of sales), a maintenance pace.
Its Rule of 40 score is 9, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
Analysts expect 8.3% long-term annual earnings growth.
own: Insiders own 40.2%, meaningful skin in the game, and institutions hold 64%.
Insiders have only bought over the past year (3 purchases).
It returns 7.3% a year to shareholders (0.4% in buybacks and 4.4% in dividends).
It pays out 119% of earnings, more than it earns, so the dividend is at risk.
Short interest is elevated at 25.1% of the float, 5.3 days to cover.
people: With about 13,500 employees, each generates about $722K of revenue, 1.4x the Consumer Defensive median.
That works out to $50K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.9M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
